analysis.one_liner: Exempts private business agreements from all federal antitrust laws.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and died in the Senate Judiciary Committee without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite the Sherman Act, the Clayton Act, and the FTC Act so they could not be applied to any voluntary agreement between individuals or companies. Because those laws are the main tools for breaking up price-fixing, market-splitting, and monopoly contracts, the bill would effectively make cartel agreements legal. It was introduced by Sen. Rand Paul, referred to the Judiciary Committee, and never taken up.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies in concentrated industries — the kind that can coordinate on prices, divide up markets, or sign contracts that squeeze suppliers, workers, and customers. Antitrust enforcement today costs some firms billions; making all private agreements exempt would let them collude without fear of federal lawsuits or FTC action.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Large firms able to coordinate prices

how_it_helps.text: Exempts every voluntary agreement among individuals or companies from the Sherman Act, Clayton Act, and FTC Act Section 5, the three pillars of federal antitrust law [S3].

Those laws are what the Justice Department and FTC use to sue price-fixing cartels, block anticompetitive mergers, and stop contracts that restrain trade; the bill says they 'shall not be construed' to reach any voluntary coordination [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and workers. Price-fixing and market-division agreements typically raise prices above competitive levels, and the loss of antitrust exposure removes the main legal deterrent. Small businesses that compete against coordinated large firms would also face markets where the rules no longer apply to bigger players.

drawbacks.text: The bill as written reaches any agreement 'entered into by or between any individual or group of individuals,' which covers classic price-fixing and market-allocation cartels — conduct both major parties' administrations have prosecuted for over a century [S3].
It offers no exception for agreements that harm consumers, so enforcement against collusive conduct would end entirely rather than being narrowed, even for the clearest cases [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Supporters of deregulating coordination argue antitrust law punishes voluntary deals and that competition is best served by government staying out. But the bill is drawn so broadly that it would shield open collusion, not just borderline conduct. The cost falls on everyone who buys goods or sells labor into markets where firms can coordinate freely.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from introduction until Congress adjourned — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Rand Paul introduced the bill on March 29, 2012 [S1].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, its only committee action [S5].
The 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, and the bill never received floor action [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and the antitrust enforcement framework — the bill's failure left price-fixing and monopoly contracts illegal, and concentrated firms gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sought its referral to the Judiciary Committee.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-VT)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill stayed in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor, no cosponsors of either party, and never left committee.

industries.note: The bill would exempt their agreements from antitrust prosecution, opening the door to coordinated pricing and market division. The cost of collusion shows up in higher prices and weaker bargaining power for workers and consumers.

industries.industry: Antitrust bar and enforcement agencies' targets
industries.note: Private antitrust litigation and DOJ/FTC enforcement would be defanged, removing legal exposure for dominant firms.
